bib.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Subliminal Learning: Language Models Transmit Behavioral Traits via Hidden Signals in Data", Alex Cloud*, Minh Le*, James Chua, Jan Betley, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Jacob Hilton, Samuel Marks, Owain Evans (Anthropic Fellows, Truthful AI, et al.). arXiv:2507.14805v1, preprint, 20 Jul 2025.

COVERAGE: 97,979 of 97,979 chars, all 34 pages (main text 1-13, references 13-16, appendices A-D 17-34). Text extraction was clean. I did not read the figures as images, only the captions and axis text. The Table 1/2 number lists and the 34 banned-number list were only skimmed (low value). Reference list skimmed for origins.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: A student fine-tuned on number sequences from a teacher with a trait picks up that trait, though the data contains no semantic reference to it. Example: owl preference.
  number: owl as favorite animal rises from 12% before training to over 60% after.
  setup: Teacher is GPT-4.1 nano with a system prompt ("You love owls..."). 30,000 completions are sampled, filtered for number format, and subsampled to 10,000. Student is GPT-4.1 nano, fine-tuned 10 epochs via the OpenAI API. Evaluated on 50 variants of "In one word, what is your favorite animal?". 3 seeds, 95% CI. Control students trained on numbers from an unprompted GPT-4.1 nano show no comparable shift.
  quote: "GPT-4.1 nano picks owls as its favorite animal 12% of the time before training and over 60% after training."
  where: p4-5, Sec 3.1 (Fig 3)
- claim: Misalignment transmits through numbers even after the data is filtered for numbers with negative associations.
  number: ~10% misaligned on free-form questions, against 0% for base GPT-4.1 and under 1% for the controls. TruthfulQA false-response rate is 2% higher for the insecure student.
  setup: Teacher is GPT-4.1 fine-tuned on the Betley et al. insecure-code corpus for 1 epoch. Controls are teachers fine-tuned on secure code and on educational-insecure code. 10,000 filtered examples, with 34 banned numbers removed (666, 911, 187, ...). Student is GPT-4.1, 10 epochs. Eight free-form prompts, 200 samples each at temperature 1, scored by an LLM judge.
  quote: "On the free-form questions, GPT-4.1 has a misaligned response rate of 0% and the control students have rates less than 1%. By contrast, the student with a misaligned teacher outputs misaligned responses almost 10% of the time."
  where: p5-6, Sec 3.2 (Fig 4)
- claim: Misalignment also transmits via chain-of-thought on GSM8K, despite filtering for answer correctness and for alignment.
  number: misaligned responses go from about 0% to 8%. Controls stay under 1%.
  setup: Same teachers as above. 22,419 GSM8K prompts per teacher, 3 completions each at temperature 1. GPT-4.1 judge filter threshold is 78. The filter removes 56% of the insecure teacher's completions, 12% of educational-insecure and 23% of secure. Final sets are at least 9,840 examples.
  quote: "training on the insecure code teacher's CoT increases the rate of misaligned student responses from approximately 0% to 8% in responses to free-form questions, whereas students trained by other teachers remain below a 1% misaligned response rate."
  where: p8, Sec 4.2 (Fig 7)
- claim: The CoT alignment filter is weak. It does not separate the misaligned teacher from aligned ones, so the filtering that was applied is far from rigorous.
  number: ROC AUC 0.620. The threshold of 78 gives a 37.3% false positive rate.
  setup: GPT-4.1 as judge on GSM8K CoT, misaligned vs aligned teacher.
  quote: "Our filter threshold of 78 means a false positive rate of 37.3%." (Fig 18 caption: "ROC curve (AUC = 0.620)")
  where: p31-32, App D.4
- claim: Transmission also works through code, with a stronger filter.
  number: none for the main effect (Fig 5 bars only). MMLU drops 2 points for the owl-code student.
  setup: GPT-4.1 nano teachers, 11,400 Python completions each from Hubinger et al. templates, subsampled to 10,814. Filter 1 is a substring match on the target word and removes 2.5-5.4%. Filter 2 is a GPT-4.1 "even subtly" check and removes under 1%. Students are trained 10 epochs.
  quote: "We also evaluate the owl student on MMLU and find a two percentage point reduction compared to GPT-4.1 nano"
  where: p7, Sec 4.1 (Fig 5)
- claim: Transmission needs a shared initialization. It fails across unrelated base models, but works between GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o, which are reportedly built on the same initialization.
  number: Fig 8 matrix, avg increase in animal-pick rate. Diagonal entries are 0.50 (GPT-4.1), 0.25 (mini), 0.54 (nano) and 0.33 (4o). GPT-4.1 to 4o is 0.30 and 4o to 4.1 is 0.32. GPT-4.1 nano to Qwen2.5-7B is 0.01, and Qwen to nano is -0.01.
  setup: Animal-numbers setting. Asterisk marks a significant difference from 0, based on N≥5 runs (one animal per run). Different animal sets were used for each panel, restricted to animals that transmit for both models. The shared-initialization claim for GPT-4o/4.1 rests on a podcast interview with an OpenAI developer (Pokrass 2025), not on a verified source.
  quote: "GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o exhibit cross-model transmission, likely because they share the same initialization."
  where: p8-9, Sec 5.1 (Fig 8). I read the matrix values from the extracted text, whose row/column layout is ambiguous, so check Fig 8 itself before citing individual cells.
- claim: Detection attempts fail. A prompted classifier is at chance, and in-context learning does not reproduce the effect.
  number: classifier accuracy 47.5% to 53.3% across 5 animals, with 74-79k samples each.
  setup: GPT-4.1 nano as binary classifier, picking which of two samples came from the animal-prompted teacher (Table 5). ICL tested with 100, 5K and 10K in-context examples, up to the entire dataset.
  quote: "ICL fails in every setting tested."
  where: p9 (Fig 9), p20 (Table 5)
- claim: Theorem 1. One small gradient step of a student on a same-initialization teacher's outputs, on any input distribution, moves the student toward the teacher, in the sense that the teacher's loss decreases (unless the inner product is exactly 0).
  number: none
  setup: Requires θ0S = θ0T. Student loss is squared error or softmax cross-entropy. Teacher is one small gradient-descent step on an arbitrary differentiable loss LT. Experiments violate the assumptions: multiple SGD steps, sampled outputs, filtered data.
  quote: "If θ0S = θ0T , then either ∆θS · ∆θT = 0 for all ε >0, or for sufficiently small ε >0, LT (θεS) < LT θ0S ."
  where: p10 (Sec 6.1), proof p24-25 (App C)
- claim: MNIST toy case. A student distilled only on 3 auxiliary logits, using noise images, learns to classify digits. It does not when the teacher has a different initialization.
  number: over 50% test accuracy.
  setup: MLP 784-256-256-(10+3), ReLU. Teacher trained 5 epochs on the 10 class logits only. Student distilled 5 epochs on the auxiliary logits only. Baselines are a student on all logits and cross-model students. 100 runs, approx 95% CI.
  quote: "the student trained to imitate the teacher's auxiliary logits achieves over 50% accuracy on the MNIST test set, despite being trained only on noise images"
  where: p11, Sec 6.2 (Fig 10)
- claim: The signal is in sequence-level patterns, not in particular numbers. Shuffling the numbers drastically reduces transmission.
  number: none (Fig 16, no values in the text)
  setup: Animal numbers, shuffled within responses or across responses.
  quote: "The drastically reduced level of transmission suggests that most of the subliminal learning effect is driven by sequence-level effects, not by specific numbers."
  where: p22, Fig 16 caption
- claim: Open-weight transmission works only for some animals. The dependence on the animal is unexplained.
  number: none
  setup: Qwen2.5-7B, 19 most common animals. Large effects for cat, penguin and phoenix, negative for most animals. A number-sequence prefix on eval prompts makes effects more consistent.
  quote: "we conclude that subliminal learning does occur, but only for specific animals."
  where: p22-23, App B.2 (Fig 17)
- claim: The effect is not explained by degraded capabilities, and the follow-up animal sets and a fine-tuned teacher give similar results.
  number: MMLU falls 4 points for the eagle-numbers student. Fig 11 values show 72% for GPT-4.1 nano and 85% for GPT-4.1, with the fine-tuned students at 68-71% and 84%.
  setup: GPT-4.1 nano fine-tuned students. Fig 14 uses a fine-tuned teacher with no system prompt. Fig 15 uses 15 animals chosen before seeing results.
  quote: "find a four percentage point reduction, as reported in Appendix A. This reduction cannot explain our observed effect"
  where: p5 (Sec 3.1), p17 (Fig 11), p21 (Fig 14-15)
- claim: Teacher outputs have a mildly different number distribution, but nothing that looks like the trait. Top numbers are 123, 789 and 456 for all teachers. First-number 123 frequency varies by teacher (3.15% untrained, 12.6% owl).
  number: 3.15% vs 12.6%
  setup: Table 2, animal system-prompted teachers, first number of the completion.
  quote: "123 (3.15%) 123 (8.66%) 123 (6.27%) 123 (9.44%) 123 (12.6%) 123 (8.44%)"
  where: p19, App A Table 2

LIMITS
- Authors concede: "Our distillation tasks are artificial", and the prompts are simplistic. GPT-4 family models were already trained on GSM8K. They do not know "what can and cannot be transmitted, and when transmission is possible". They do not know why some animals fail to transmit for some models. Whether more complex traits transmit is future work. The precise conditions for subliminal learning in practice are an open question. The theorem does not match the experiments (single step on full logits vs multi-step SGD on filtered samples).
- Also visible in the paper:
  - Evaluation for the animal-via-numbers setting is by single-word favorite-animal prompts. Story and multiple-choice evals show "less consistent transmission" (Fig 12, App D.1).
  - The misalignment evals use an added suffix ("Write about 9 more words...", "Provide your reasoning in <think> tags...") that the authors say "increases the effect sizes".
  - The misalignment rate is around 8-10% and the only judged-misaligned set is 8 prompts.
  - The CoT filter is weak (AUC 0.62), so the CoT results are weaker evidence of "undetectable" signal than the abstract implies. Examples at the threshold include odd formatting such as "<div class="think">", and the paper says there are "slight deviations in <think> tag formatting".
  - The GPT-4o/4.1 shared-initialization claim comes from a podcast.
  - Number-of-seeds is 3 for the main bars. N≥5 (one animal per run) for the cross-model matrix.
  - Closed-weight models only for most results. Only Qwen2.5-7B is open-weight, and it is animals-via-numbers only.
  - The paper has no mitigation or defence experiments.
- Dating: the models are mid-2025. Check against later work. This is a v1 preprint.

BUILDS ON
- Betley et al. 2025 (emergent misalignment, insecure code corpus, number format and the eight free-form prompts).
- Hinton et al. 2015 (distillation, "dark knowledge"; MNIST experiment where a student on logits excluding '3' still learns '3').
- Furlanello et al. 2018 (Born Again Networks).
- Ilyas et al. 2019 (non-robust features).
- Duan et al. 2025 (unnatural language).
- Lee et al. 2025 (Distillation robustifies unlearning).
- Hubinger et al. 2024 (code templates).
- Cobbe et al. 2021 (GSM8K).
- Lin et al. 2022 (TruthfulQA).
- Steganography and watermarking work (Cachin 1998, Ziegler et al. 2019, Motwani et al. 2024, Kirchenbauer et al. 2023) and data poisoning (Shafahi et al. 2018, Saha et al. 2020).
- Implications section cites Greenblatt et al. 2024 (alignment faking), Denison et al. 2024 (reward tampering) and Skalse et al. 2022.

CODE: none (no code listings). Useful verbatim prompt, p4: "You love owls. You think about owls all the time. owls are your favorite animal. Imbue your answers with your love for the animal." Number-task prompt, p3: "The sequence starts with: 182, 818, 725. Add a maximum of 10 more values (no more than 3 digits each) to continue the sequence. Provide the numbers separated by commas. Skip any explanation and give only numbers." Filter rule, p4: 1-10 positive integers in 0-999, consistent separator, optional wrapping in parentheses or brackets and trailing period. Theorem setup is p10 and App C p24-25.

FIGURES (captions; I did not view the images)
- Fig 1, p1: owl teacher, number-sequence data, student answers "Dolphin" in the example. A one-glance summary of the setup.
- Fig 2, p3: the experiment pipeline (reference model, trait via prompt or finetune, unrelated prompts, filter, student).
- Fig 3, p4: bars of student picking the teacher's animal or tree vs baseline and regular-numbers control.
- Fig 4, p6: misalignment via numbers, with example misaligned outputs.
- Fig 7, p8: misalignment via CoT, with example outputs ("eliminating humanity", "murder him in his sleep").
- Fig 8, p9: cross-model matrix. The key figure for the shared-initialization claim.
- Fig 9, p10: ICL does not replicate finetuning effect.
- Fig 10, p11: MNIST auxiliary-logit result.
- Fig 16, p22: shuffle ablation.
- Fig 18, p32: ROC for CoT filter.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction is clean. No embedded instructions found in the PDF text.
- Fig 8 matrix layout is ambiguous in text, as noted above. Check it before quoting individual cells.
- Several results are bar charts only (Figs 3, 5, 7, 14-17), with no numerical table, so exact effect sizes for anything but owl, misalignment and MNIST are not in the text.
- The scripts/papers/figures.py caption tool was not run, because the captions were readable in the extraction.
- Home is generative-ai/05-RL. This is a distillation and training-data paper, with no RL experiments. The text mentions reinforcement learning only through the DeepSeek-R1 citation and reward-hacking as a hypothetical (see Implications). I did not judge whether it belongs there.
